Yes. 

The story sets up the expectation of an abandoned, neglected house following the solitary death of Hanna's mother (the moss-covered flowerpot, the twenty-year absence, the expectation of a rusty lock). The turn comes when the lock turns effortlessly, revealing fresh machine oil that smells specifically like her father's workshop—a subject that was taboo in the house—followed by the discovery that someone has recently swept and removed the rugs. This is surprising because it subverts the trope of the untouched, decaying estate and introduces an unexpected, mysterious presence (possibly the estranged father). At the same time, it is entirely appropriate: it fits the quiet, realistic, and melancholic tone of a story about estranged family histories, and it was subtly foreshadowed by the mowed lawn mentioned in the second paragraph.
